title: Why You're 1 cm Taller Every Morning 📏
description:
Why are you taller in the morning than at night? All day, gravity squeezes water out of the 23 squishy discs in your spine so you shrink about a centimeter by bedtime, and while you sleep the discs soak water back up like sponges.

topic: Why are you taller in the morning than at night?
script: You lose one centimeter of height every day, but why? Your spine isn't one solid bone. It's a stack of vertebrae, with twenty-three squishy discs in between. Each disc is like a jelly doughnut, with a soft, watery middle. All day, gravity pushes down on you. Every step and every sit squeezes a little water out, and the discs flatten a tiny bit. Add up all twenty-three, and you've shrunk about a centimeter by bedtime. But when you lie down to sleep, the weight comes off your spine. The discs soak water back up, like little sponges, and by morning, you're tall again. In space, with no gravity, astronauts can grow three percent taller! So tonight, measure yourself before bed, then again when you wake up. Will you be one centimeter taller tomorrow morning?
key_facts: The intervertebral discs between vertebrae compress under load during the day, so people are typically around 1 cm (often quoted up to about 2 cm) shorter by evening (scienceblog; mechse.illinois.edu)
The adult spine has 23 intervertebral discs, each with a tough outer ring (annulus fibrosus) and a soft, water-rich gel centre (nucleus pulposus)
Lying down removes the load and the discs rehydrate overnight, restoring height by morning
Without gravity, astronauts' spines lengthen and they can grow up to about 3% taller in space (Scientific American; Space.com)
